utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. And welcome back, after a break, which and I'm sure we will -- we have all returned with a determination to get on with it. If any of you happened to be at the opening of the ILA conference this morning, you would have heard one of the speakers did not let the opportunity pass to talk about how much time these criminal Tribunals take so that I'm sure that we -- would make a determined effort in short that in terms of this trial in this Tribunal, that we will be the exception to this universal criticism which tends to be immediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene and but my colleague tells me that this is an -- there was no interpretation in Serbian, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it okay now? Yes. Okay. So could we have the appearances, please. And for those you that just missed what I just said, I just said that I'm sure that we are going to speed up the work now that we are in the final stage of this trial, to be an example to other Tribunals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis along with Gerard Dobbyn and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Igor Pantelic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, there are three matters which the Chamber would wish to bring to the attention of the parties. The first is a reminder to the Prosecution that the witness which who is scheduled for this afternoon, witness number 63, is a Rule -- sorry, 92 ter witness for whom we have already ruled there would be -- that the time for examination-in-chief would be limited to 30 minutes. And we do -- we are not -- we haven't forgotten the indication that the counsel respectively for each of the accused indicated that they are likely to take in terms of their cross-examination. The second matter is the proposal for some of the 44 new witnesses to address the denied adjudicated facts and we would respectfully urge the Prosecution to let us have on an urgent basis the highlighted statements and less important, and that's, of course, the Defence, because the highlighted portions of the statements so much depends on -- on where we go with those witnesses. The third thing is that the Trial Chamber -- the -- does require that the estimates for all of these witnesses, including those who may be admitted pursuant to 92 bis that we would need that to be provided to us. And unless council have any matters themselves to raise, could the usher -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I do. And if it is convenient for the Court now I can do it now or later, whichever you prefer. Two matters, Your Honour, one related just for scheduling for this week. The first witness is Witness ST-063, is here, ready to start. I think Mr. Dobbyn has an application to make concerning that witness and I will leave that to him. Tomorrow's witness is ST-134. On Wednesday we had ST-163 scheduled, but last week a problem arose. We learned that he testified in the state court in Bosnia in two matters, including one involving a witness we had here, ST-187. We have been attempting to get the transcripts of his testimony from those two cases. We just received one on Friday. The other, I think, has been requested, but we don't know if one had even been prepared. It is my understanding that they aren't always prepared for those trials and without having that transport in hand we didn't think it was convenient for the witness or the parties to proceed with him because his testimony related to directly to this case and to a witness who has previously testified in this case. So Wednesday we don't currently have a witness scheduled. The witness for Thursday is ST-147. We can't move him up because is he travelling by car rather than aeroplane and won't be here until Wednesday evening and won't be able to start testifying until Thursday. I think Ms. Pidwell had sent an e-mail to the Legal Officer asking about the possibility of swapping Friday and Wednesday because Friday is a day that you're not sitting. But I think as of this late date that is not probably not a feasibility possibility. So we propose to proceed in that fashion. We think we can get ST-147 done on Thursday. If that is the only day we sit with him. I think the Prosecution has 20 minutes in direct. He's a 92 ter witness, and the Defence has estimated three and a half hours. So we should be able just possibly to squeeze him in. The second matter I wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just in relation to the proposal you just made, would you be able to bring another witness for Friday then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but what we thought would happen is that in the event that we carry over into Wednesday with the first two witnesses, then we wouldn't -- we wouldn't have any problem hopefully completing all three this week. Our concern is if we didn't finish with the second witness tomorrow, ST-134, that might spill over into Thursday and that would force ST-147 to spill over into the following week or some later day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. If he didn't finish tomorrow's witness you said it would spill over into Thursday, why not Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] we're hear witness, no problem [Microphone not activated]. The 44 new witnesses regarding adjudicated facts, I think the -- the Court had requested we keep you updated on our process in making disclosure pertinent to those two witnesses. We will tell that you the first batch of disclosure went out on the 10th August involving ten of those witnesses concerning our review of the updated ISU searches that we conduct. The second batch will go out either today or tomorrow and that covers a further eight witnesses. So that's 18 by tomorrow. And we hope to have another batch out on Friday. And we've heard what you have said this morning, or just at the beginning of this session, about getting the highlighted statements and transcripts to you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be heard on the same subject, Your Honours. We filed a motion on the 4th of August requesting that we -- that we are provided with the -- with the 92 bis packages for these witnesses, because, Your Honours, you gave us the deadline of the 20th of August. But we, as of today, we still haven't received that. So if we don't receive it in any -- any time very soon, we wouldn't be able to -- to give our response by the 20th of August. So that is -- that is why we filed the motion as early as 4th of August. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- the -- you haven't forgotten that the deadline was extended to the 3rd of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I obviously forgot that, Your Honours. I'm sorry. We were -- the whole team was -- had the understanding that the -- that the deadline was the 20th of August. I'm really sorry. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly, Your Honours, concerning Wednesday. If we are not sitting with the witness on Wednesday, we propose to meet with the Defence counsel to discuss a couple of matters, including possible agreements about something regarding these 44 adjudicated facts witnesses and 92 bis statements for some of them and also matters concerning the exhumation evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to make sure that there is no misunderstanding anymore about the Court's order to give estimates for the witnesses you proposed to be 92 bis, to give estimates, time estimates for them to be heard eventually as viva voce witnesses. Because we -- as you probably remember, we -- we already ordered that twice, once written and once in your presence orally. You said they would -- they would be provided -- it would be provided for very soon. And then we got a motion from your office telling us the opposite. So we are emphasising that we would like to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it sounds like we had an internal miscommunication. I understand you now. You wanted us to estimate how much time we would need for those witnesses proposed as 92 bis in the event that you decide that they need to come and testify live and we need to present their evidence, their direct evidence live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With this clear understanding that these witnesses are only there to testify about the specific denied adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I anticipate though that if some of those do come that we have listed to testify to a particular adjudicated fact, we would feel an obligation to expand a little farther than answering one question. For example, who were the perpetrators at this incident on the 19th July, 1992, the police. We think you would need to hear a little more from this witness as to who they were and how they happened to know it was the police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I trusts that we are not at cross purposes. It may very well be that you and the Bench are saying the same thing. But bearing in mind that the purpose for which these witnesses -- each of those witnesses being called is to deal with specific facts which would have been identified by the Prosecution in its several motions for the -- for the acceptance of these matters as adjudicated facts, that, whereas, if I understand you correctly, that narrowly speaking, there are, of course, would have to be a context to the evidence but the basic and -- we cannot overemphasise the fact that these witnesses are being called for the limited purpose of speaking viva voce to the particular issues which would have been identified by the Prosecution and notified to the other side and the Chamber as being important to their case by virtue of the original motions for the -- for the reception of these matters as adjudicated facts. As I said, I trust we are not at cross purposes in that regard but that is the basal position of the Chamber in terms of that regard, and that is a point to which we would firmly hold and any attempt to wander outside of -- of those limitations will be firmly shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we are not at cross purposes. I think I understand what you are saying. You said the word "context," and I guess that's the word I should have used. I think we're on the same page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you give us an indication about when we could have these estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I could probably give you an indication by the end of the day. I guess I personally need to go back and look at how many we propose in 92 bis and try and come up with a rough estimate for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, could the usher have the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. I trust that can you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The solemn declaration that you would have made binds you to speak truthfully to this Tribunal, which has the power to deal with misleading or untruthful testimony by way of its powers to punish persons for perjury. Would you begin by telling us your name, your date of birth, your profession and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nusret Sivac. I was born on the 19th of August, 1947. And I'm currently unemployed. In fact, I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] what was your profession before you were retired? You may have said it, but I didn't have the translation because I was set on the wrong channel. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 1st of January, 1990, I was an employee of the public security service in Prijedor. And as of January 1st, 1990, through May 1992, I was a reporter for the Sarajevo Television, and I covered certain municipalities in the western portion of the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And you would have testified previously before this Tribunal, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would remind you of the procedure with which you would be familiar from your previous testimony. The side calling you would begin by asking you questions and then the other side, counsel for each of the two accused would have a right to cross-examine you, and which the Prosecution could re-examine and, at that stage or indeed at any earlier stage in your testimony, the Bench my intervene if they have questions of you. The procedure under which you are being called is such that the Prosecution would be completed with their examination-in-chief in 30 minutes, and the Defence together have indicated such a period of time for your cross-examination that it is fully expected that your testimony would be completed before the Chamber rises for the day at 7.00 this evening. The -- there are the Tribunal sits for periods of not more than an hour and a half for certain technical reasons dealing with the changing of the tapes by which these proceedings are recorded. But if at any time before the usual point for a break arises, you need of any reason to have a break in your testimony if you would indicate that to the Chamber and, of course, we would accommodate you. And with that, I would invite Mr. Hannis to begin his examination-in-chief. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Dobbyn will be leading this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. And before I start and I am keeping in mind the comments at the start of court today, I am actually going to be requesting an additional 30 minutes with this witness for a total of one hour. And the reason for that is when Mr. Sivac was brought in for proofing on Saturday, he did raise some matters concerning meetings that were attended by the accused Stojan Zupljanin in Prijedor in the relevant time-period and they are uncontained in his 92 ter statement. And we produced a proofing note which was disclosed to the Defence. That's one reason we're asking additional time. Also, Your Honours, back on I believe the 13th of July, counsel for the accused Zupljanin had indicated that there was specifically challenging certain adjudicated facts, three in particular, and these were adjudicated facts that this witness speaks to, so I would like to spend a short amount of additional time on that. Keeping in mind, I'm asking for a total of an hour at the most. I hope to finish before that. And I think still with the times given for cross-examination we would be able to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, we have heard your application for an additional time beyond the 30 minutes indicated, and we will allow you 20 minutes. So it would be a total of 50 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac. As you've heard we have 50 minutes today. So I just ask that when I do ask you questions that you answer as concisely as possible so that we can cover as many of the areas that I would to as we can. Now, Mr. Sivac, did you testify in the Stakic case on the 29th, 30th and 31st of August and the 1st of September, 2002, and also on the 13th of January, 2003?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you also testify in the Brdjanin case on the 13th and 14th of January, 2003?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in particular on 13th of January, 2003, in the Brdjanin case, do you recall correcting earlier testimony you'd given in the Stakic case with regards to a delegations of Bosnian Serb officials who had visited Omarska camp in July 1992 and you recall saying that you had mistaken said that Vojo Kupresanin was part of this delegation when, in fact, it was Stojan Zupljanin. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now have you had a chance to listen to the testimony you gave in Stakic and Brdjanin before today?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is the information contained in that testimony, keeping in mind the correction that I have just referred to, would the answers you give today, if you testified in full, be the same as you gave in those two cases?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. My testimony and my statements, I stand by them, and I -- I firmly state that Mr. Zupljanin, in 1992, together with a political delegation of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, led by Mr. Brdjanin, that they visited the camp in Omarska and the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I believe the procedure is that upon the completion of his testimony I would seek to tender thinks 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, now if could I read a very brief summary of his 92 ter testimony. Mr. Sivac is a Bosnian Muslim who until 1990 worked for the public security service in Prijedor and in 1992 was working as a television reporter in Prijedor. His 92 ter testimony provides an overview of the Serb takeover of Prijedor in April 1992, the persecution of non-Serbs in Prijedor and the destruction of non-Serb religious buildings and property. Mr. Sivac was present in Prijedor on 30th May, 1992, when the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor began. He saw non-Serbs being taken from their homes by the Serb forces who separated the men from the women and children before taking them away. He witnessed the looting and destruction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please read more slowly for the benefit of interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise to the interpreters. I will slow down. He witnessed the looting and destruction of non-Serb homes and religious buildings. On 10 June 1992, Mr. Sivac was arrested by Serb police. He was taken to the Prijedor SUP building and transported to Keraterm and then on to Omarska. En route to Omarska he witnessed the devastation of the Kozarac area with houses burning and personal possessions and dead animals scattered across the road. He was beaten upon arrival at Omarska but released that same day when told that, in fact, it was his sister who was to have been arrested. Mr. Sivac was arrested again on 20 June 1992 and returned to Omarska. In his 92 ter testimony, he described the brutal and inhumane conditions at Omarska including beatings, killings, insufficient food and lack of sanitary facilities. In July 1992, Mr. Sivac witnessed the visit to the delegation of high-ranking Bosnian Serb officials to Omarska camp. This delegation included Radoslav Brdjanin, Simo Miskovic, Simo Drljaca and Stojan Zupljanin. Along with the other prisoners, Mr. Sivac was made to line up before this delegation and was forced to sing Serbian songs. Mr. Sivac was transferred to Trnopolje camp in August 1992 where he remained for 14 days. Upon his release, he returned to Prijedor where he remained until he was finally able, after signing over all his property, to leave in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I'm now going to ask you some questions just to clarify and expand upon these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: First of all, if we could show 65 ter 3111.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, what you see coming up on the screen in front of you is a map of the municipality of Prijedor. I'll just wait until it's increased in size. Now, Mr. Sivac, you will see that it features many of the locations that you mention in your testimony, including Prijedor town Hambarine, Kozarac, Keraterm camp, Trnopolje, and Omarska. Mr. Sivac, looking at that map, is that an accurate depiction of the municipality of Prijedor and does it show the correct locations of these places?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I would like to tender this map at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 01 -- P01526. Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, are you -- were you aware of any visits by Stojan Zupljanin to Prijedor in the weeks leading up to the takeover on 30th of April, and in particular I'm looking at the date around the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Around the 10th of April, my colleague, a journalist, Mr. Grubic, who was a Serb, was also a member of the Patriot League in Prijedor. They were for peace. However, he received information from Banja Luka that Stojan Zupljanin was to visit Prijedor, accompanied by Radoslav Brdjanin. Their aim was to hold discussions at the municipal building with the -- the authorities about the way the local police would be divided. I'm trying to speak slowly enough for the interpreters. There was a group of members of the Patriot League which gathered people of all ethnicity, including my colleague, Mr. Grubic as well as Dr. Eso Sadikovic and Nina Cacic, i.e., all those people were of different ethnicities, and they stood in front of the municipal building there Prijedor stating that they would not see the Prijedor police be divided or split up. I'm saying this because in the municipality of Prijedor, the legally-elected representatives were still in power. It was Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, who was the municipal president, as well Mr. Stakic, who was his deputy. The president of the executive board was Mr. Mico Kovacevic. The chief of the security service in Prijedor was Hasan Talundzic. When they realised that a group of citizens spontaneously gathered in front of the municipal building, somebody from the municipal building decided that the gentlemen from Banja Luka should not enter the building through the main door. They actually entered through the back door, holding a meeting at which they failed to convince those in power, in Prijedor, to split up the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, if I could just ask you at this point, Mr. Sivac, you've said that Mr. Zupljanin -- that the purpose of the visit was to seek the division of the police. On what basis or on what lines was he seeking the division of the police?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, at the time the goal was clearly recognisable. They were there to put up an ultimatum for it to be done in, as they called it, in a peaceful way. However, only some 20 days later, there was going to be a forcible takeover by the police and army in the municipality of Prijedor. This had already been planned back then. However, for pro forma sake, in order to wash their hands of certain events that were to ensue, they attempted to persuade, so to speak, those in power in the municipality of Prijedor to tackle those issues in the municipality by dividing the police among its Muslim and Serb fractions. The next day, dissatisfied with the outcome of the talks, the Banja Luka and Prijedor media carried the following news and they were all controlled by the Serbian Democratic Party that was in power then, and trying to raise tensions among the ethnicities, they stated that -- that there had been an assassination planned against Zupljanin and others in Prijedor. But this was only done in order to raise the bar, so to speak, to have the Serbs readied for what was to ensue some 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivac. And, again, just because of the time constraints, I'd ask you to just try to keep it as concise as possible, your answers. Now, after the takeover, the Serb takeover of Prijedor on the 30th of April, are you aware of Mr. Zupljanin attending any meetings in the days shortly after that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After the takeover, there was another group of Banja Luka politicians, including Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, which arrived in the iron ore complex, they set up -- they held a meeting. This is vis-a-vis the SUP building. The meeting was with certain employees of the security service. At that meeting, it was stated that all non-Serb employees, that is to say, Muslims and Croats, if they wanted to remain with the security service, had to sign a loyalty oath to the new Serb authorities. At that meeting, there was a very small number of Muslims and Croats in attendance, because, already, during the takeover, they had been driven away, sent away from their jobs. However, at that meeting, and the explanation that if the non-Serbs wanted to remain with the Serb security service, had to sign the security oath was just a farce. I know for sure that several Muslims and Croats, indeed, signed it. However, it didn't help them any. They were still taken to the Omarska and Keraterm camps and killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivac, in May 1992, did you hear any information about negotiations concerning the situation in Kozarac taking place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There was a large problem facing the new people in power in Banja Luka and Prijedor, and that was how to deal with the situation in Kozarac. Kozarac is a small village adjacent to Prijedor which had always remained with the security service of Prijedor. They rejected any ultimatums coming from Banja Luka rejecting the new power structures there. 95 per cent of Kozarac -- 95 per cent of the population of Kozarac were Muslims. They rejected all ultimatums and they would not recognise the newly appointed people in Prijedor who found themselves in the positions after the forcible take over. Instead, they self-organised to try and talk the Kozarac police into accepting the new people in Prijedor. We received information that Stojan Zupljanin attempted again to go to Kozarac, accompanied by some other politicians in order to reduce tensions so that the Kozarac police be persuaded to join the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was -- what was the source of this information, Mr. Sivac?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We received that information from our colleagues in Banja Luka. My colleague, Boro Grubic, a Serb journalist who worked with me, got by that information when Osmo Didovic, who was then the Kozarac police station commander, rejected all previous ultimatums. He said that there were bad things in store for Kozarac and that the situation in Kozarac, as such, was no longer tenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what was the outcome of these negotiations that Stojan Zupljanin took part in?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. Information reached us that any negotiations about a peaceful handover of Kozarac and accepting the new Serb authorities failed and that they were going back to Banja Luka without anything having been done. On the other hand, from the political circles of Prijedor, there were Milomir Stakic and Simo Drljaca who also took part in those negotiations with the police and the people of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: How long after these negotiations failed to reach any result did the cleansing of Kozarac begin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It lasted for about ten days. Some ten days later, that is to say, around the 24th of May, 1992, the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac began.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to another topic now. In Stakic, you testified that both of the times you were arrested in June 1992, you were transported from the Prijedor SUP building to Omarska in what you described as a standard police paddy wagon. I just got a couple of specific questions about that. What colour was the vehicle? I'm sorry, have you heard the question, Mr. Sivac? I'll repeat it again. The question was: What colour was the vehicle you were transported in?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I heard the question. It was a typical police van. It was dark blue in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did it have any markings on it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think the markings were still "milicija" on the door. I can't recall precisely though. I am quite familiar with such vans. I have been with the security service for 20 years, and I remember when that particular van was purchased. Some work-mates of mine mounted radio equipment in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Specifically referring to your first arrest on the 10th of June, you testified that you were transported by Tomislav Stojakovic and Rade Balta. What organ, if any, did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They used to be work-mates with mine with whom I had worked for a number of years. They were professional policemen from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The second time you were driven from the SUP building to Omarska on the 20th of June, do you know the names of the men who took you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The driver was Stevo Grahovac, another professional policeman who used to be a good work-mate of mine. The co-driver was a reserve policeman. I don't know his exact name but we used to refer to him as -- Batan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last piece of information he offered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a reserve policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, just for the record, Your Honours, that was in response to the challenge of adjudicated fact, 858. Now if we could call up 65 ter 2237.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, do you recognise the building on the -- in the picture in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the security service building in Prijedor. I had worked there for about 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is this the building you were taken to after your two arrests?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In Stakic you described how you and some others, including you and young boy, were forced to run a gauntlet, this is after your arrest on 20 June during which members of the Prijedor Intervention Platoon beat you with metal bars. In this photo, can you see the area where that happened?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One cannot see it here. This is the frontal part of the building, and we were taken through the main door to the back where there's a yard. In the yard, in front of detention cells, four of us were lined up in front of a wall. Before that they took our shoe laces away as well as our belts, they removed all -- the documents and money we had. We stood next to the wall with our hands on our -- on the back of our heads, and that is where the members of the Intervention Platoon started beating up. It was around noon. All of my former Serbian colleagues who were still with the security service looked on from the windows that were facing the yard. They were all laughing. Perhaps I should tell this to the Judges. Next to me there was another former employee who was a white-colour inspector. He was arrested with me with other two colleagues and while the beating took place, and it was quite heavy, it all seemed very funny to our former colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I would seek to tender this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01527, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Next could we show 65 ter 2234.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, can you tell the Court what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is a panoramic view of the iron ore mine in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I'd like your help in locating and marking a few specific places you talk about in your prior testimony. You testified that when you arrived at Omarska for the second time on 20th of June, you were lined up against the wall of the restaurant and beaten by guards. Now with the usher's assistance, I'd ask you to indicate where that -- that restaurant was. If you could perhaps mark it with a cross.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Apologies. The second time we arrived in Omarska, the Omarska sentries did not beat us. Kos Krle was the guard's commander and he said, These had already been beaten enough today. Do not beat them any further. We arrived in a van and were lined up next to this wall of the restaurant. It had glass window-panes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could put the number 1 next to that cross, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, this restaurant, is this also where you were taken for your meals?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: From your testimony you stated that initially you were held in the garage. Could you mark where the garage is, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken this way. The garage is at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could put the number 2, just near the front of the building where the arrow goes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, here is the number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You also spent some time in places known as Burho's room and Mujo's room. Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One cannot see it here. It is somewhere here on the back side, and can I mark it with a 3. It was next to the interrogation rooms. The entrance is from that side of the building, next to the garage, and that's where the two room are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Speaking of the interrogations rooms, could you mark where they were, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: On this side. These were the windows, as well as at the other side of the building. This is where the interrogation rooms were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: On the top floor. This used to be the management building of the mine in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just for the record, I'll say that that's indicated by four crosses on either side of the building which has numbers 2 and 3 by it, now marked with number 4. Now, Mr. Sivac, you also described how at night you could hear the sounds of female prisoners screaming, crying, and calling for help. Where were they held? Where were these screams coming from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In day-time, the women were in the restaurant. They were there to assist the personnel in the restaurant, to give food to the inmates. In the evening, after 7.00 p.m. when the night shift came in, they were taken to sleep in the interrogation rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay, and these are the rooms that you've marked with the crosses and number 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were divided into two groups in two different rooms among the total of the interrogation rooms that there were. This is where they spent their nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You've also described that the detainees were held in the hangar. Could you please marked hangar with the number 5?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There is the hangar. All of it. Here's the number 5. The detainees were both in the upper and the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You've also testified that detainees were held and killed in the white house. Could you mark that with a number 6, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the notorious white house. This is a number 6 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In your testimony you also referred to the red house. Could you mark that, please, with a number 7.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That is the red house. The detainees were killed there in a quiet way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by "killed in a quiet way"?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Detainees were killed there with hammers, axes, and other instruments of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, also, you have referred in your testimony to the glass house. Could you locate this on this picture?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It will be difficult. It's between the management building and the restaurant. There's a rectangular room there without a roof. It is just fenced off by glass panes. This is what it is, and it's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you've marked that with the number 8, I see. Finally, you described how, upon your rival at Omarska on the 10th of June, you saw a huge number of prisoners lying face down on the area known as the pista, and you also described having spent time lying there yourself. Could you locate the pista on this picture?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the pista. I'm marking it with a 9. Detainees were lined up like this on the ground out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I tender this photograph now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the marked portion of 65 ter 02234 shall be given Exhibit P01528. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I'm going to move on to the issue of the -- the visit of this delegation to Omarska. And you talked about this in both Stakic and Brdjanin. And at the start of your testimony today, we covered the fact that Stojan Zupljanin had been part of this delegation along with Vojin Kupresanin. Now, Mr. Sivac, in 1992, did you know who Mr. Zupljanin was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In 1992, I knew the following: I knew this man because he appeared on television frequently, and during some police operations orchestrated from the centres for security services this gentleman would voice his opinion and the purpose and results of the operation that had been carried out. Although -- although in my first testimony I said that he and Mr. Kupresanin were a bit alike and I couldn't really tell them apart too well at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now you said that you couldn't tell them apart too well at the time. But at that time that the delegation visited -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there is something missing in the transcription, the name of these two gentlemen, I think. Mr. Kupresanin, was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I see the mention of Mr. Kupresanin at line 21 and carrying on to line 22. Was there another place besides that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you said that you couldn't really tell them apart too well, Mr. Sivac, were you referring to Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. During the time when the delegation visited Omarska, at that time, I was sure about who it was. At that time, I knew that this was in fact Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: It has been some time obviously since that day back in July 1992, but I'd ask you to take your time and look around the courtroom and can you tell us if you see Stojan Zupljanin in the court today?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. That's the gentleman sitting on my left side and he has a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record he has indicated the accused Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivac, you described that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose of that? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the line of questioning whether this was Zupljanin and whether he could recognise him, whether he saw this gentleman, whether he could see him here in the courtroom, I think these -- I don't see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point of it was that unless the accused counsel are willing to agree that Mr. Zupljanin was present at the time, this goes to the weight that should be given to the witness's identification at that time of the accused Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For myself, Mr. Krgovic, I was -- my mild surprise of the question which, on the face of it, was an invitation to dock identification, was relieved by interpreting it, and I believe this is how it was intended as a formal question to link the testimony. In other words, he is not seeking to establish the -- what other circumstances would be identification for the first time. So nothing turns on it. Yes, Mr. Dobbyn, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you described while this delegation visited, being forced to sing Serbian songs and give the Serbian three-fingered salute. How did the members of this delegation react to this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, they laughed. That was their reaction. They couldn't believe that this large number of men, the entire "intelligentsia" of Prijedor at the time was so mortified and was so helpless and that they were forced to sing the Serbian Chetnik songs and give the three-fingered absolute and call out, This is Serbia, this is Serbia. For us, this was humiliating, and for the men who are members of this delegation, they found that funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you describe the appearance of detainees at the time?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: At the time, the camp inmates looked really miserable and they all had obvious and visible signs of abuse. They were very skinny. And many of them had been ill, had fallen ill, because of the poor conditions in the rooms where they were kept. So they looked really poor -- they looked bad and miserable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we now show 65 ter 2232.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, we cannot access 65 ter 2322 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: 2232. And, sorry, it should be 22 -- 2233. We do have it in Sanction, if that will help matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sivac, and Your Honours, this picture is a still frame shot from the video that has already been admitted as P1538, a video shot at Omarska. Mr. Sivac, looking at the physical condition of this man, how typical was this of the prisoners at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is what they looked like, even worse. There were men who couldn't even get up on their feet. That's how emaciated and beaten up they were. They couldn't even stand on their feet. And the, thanks to Burho and Mujo who were in our room, who had the courage to go and ask for some bread for them so they wouldn't die of hunger lying there in the rooms, because they couldn't go attend that one single meal. As for the man behind this emaciated man in white, he was the -- he was a lawyer in Prijedor. I believe his name was Basic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could I tender --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: And he was the secretary of the Executive Council in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I tender this photograph now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01529. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, in Stakic you mentioned a guard named Mladjo Radic. How did you know Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we used to work together in the security service. He was an active duty police officer, and when necessary, he would be transferred to the police stations in Ljubija and Prijedor, and then toward the end, just before 1992, he was assigned to work in the police station in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now what position, if any, did he hold at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: He was one of the shift commanders. The worst shift in the Omarska camp during which time, and understand his -- while he was the commander of that shift, the greatest number of killings and rapes of women occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you, on any occasion, speak to him at Omarska camp; and, if so, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Once, when -- while we were returning from this meal, in the hallway, I ran into Mladjo Radic, with whom I used to be close friends for a while, I stopped briefly and asked him, Mladjo, tell me, what is going to happen with us? And he replied, short and brief, Sivac, there is no help. All of you here are slated for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now move on. In Stakic, you testified that you were transferred from Omarska to Trnopolje on the 7th of August, 1992. And I'd like to show 65 ter 2483. Mr. Sivac, do you recognise what's shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is a view of the co-operative, the farmer's co-operative in Trnopolje. And on the right-hand side, this larger building, that was the elementary school there Trnopolje. And in fact that was where the Trnopolje camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now there appear to be two buildings here, two main buildings, one on left and one on the right, both coloured white. Were detainees held in both buildings?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They were head held in both these buildings and there is another building that is not shown in the photo here. It is about -- in that direction. This was a rather run-down building, which used to house a shop selling construction materials and there were some sheds attached to it where some wooden boards were kept, and this is where camp inmates were held too. But the largest number of inmates were actually held here, and I will mark the area where the fence ran. It ran along this line that I marked. The largest number of camp inmates were held in this area outdoors in the open, because not all of us could actually fit in all the facilities that were here. So we were out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this with the marks on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01530. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we're at the point for the break, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness comes in, I have been asked to forward the request that we be able to formally excuse the next witness for the rest of the day, ST-134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand the gremlins have been added this afternoon and we have to re-do an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's the -- sorry. P1528 which was the map, sorry, the photograph of Omarska with the various markings on, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In case you have not been alerted, Mr. Dobbyn, the 50 minutes that the Chamber had allowed you on your application, you have exhausted 52 of those 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. If I could seek your indulgence. I have just one photograph, which will perhaps take two or three minutes, and then to re -- go over the problematic photograph again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I have one final picture that I'd like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 2240.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, again, this is a still frame taken from Exhibit P1583 from a segment that was shot at Trnopolje camp. Mr. Sivac, do you recognise anyone in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my best friend from Prijedor, Ahmed Djulkic [phoen]. He was a plumber in Prijedor. And next to him I believe is Penny Marshall. Now, Your Honours, you can see here that -- what can you see in the background where you see this makeshift, some kind of tarp, this is where the -- this is where we were kept in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, the physical condition of your friend, Mr. Djulkic, was it common to see people in that sort of condition in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Ahmed Djulkic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. This is what the inmates looked like, the camp inmates who had been transferred from Omarska and Keraterm to Trnopolje. Most of the time this is what they looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this picture now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, as the witness says that this is one of his friends, he could perhaps tell us how the man looked like before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I wonder if you heard His Honour Judge Delvoie's question. Could you compare the condition of Mr. Djulkic in this photo to how he had been before he was held in the -- at the detention camps?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I said this precisely because I had known him very well before he was brought to the camp. He looked very well, and he was very well built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now I have nothing further that I was going to cover with you with the time available, Mr. Sivac. However, there was a technical problem. The photograph showing Omarska camp that you made several markings on, there was -- as I say, a technical problem, and your markings weren't saved, so we will have to go over that again as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if we could call again 65 ter 2234.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now you identified this earlier as being a panoramic photograph of Omarska camp. You marked the wall of the restaurant with a cross and a number 1. Could you mark that again, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's number 1. Here it is. So I've done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You also marked the garage where you were held with the number 2. Could you do that again, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's here on this side. Number 2 is where the garage was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you mark again Burho's room and Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want me to mark? I'm sorry, I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you mark Burho's room -- [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it right here, a room down here, number 3. It's at the lower level of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one second. [B/C/S on English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Next, could you marked the interrogations [sic] rooms?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I will mark it. That's here, the upper level, where you see the windows of these buildings. That is above Burho's and Mujo's rooms in the garage area. Let's put number 4 there. There were a number of offices where the inmates were questioned and during the night those rooms were used for accommodating woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: The next pace you marked was the hangar and you marked that with a number 5. Could you do that again, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the building here. Number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could you mark the white house again, please, with the number 6.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The white house, right here, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And the red house with number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Seven, the red house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You also indicated where the glass house was. If you could indicate that again and mark it with a number 8.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's right here, between the administration building and the cafeteria. So that is number 8. And this area which I will mark with number 9, that's where the notorious pista was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's all the places we had marked earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So I would seek to tender this again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document had already been marked as Exhibit P01528. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sivac. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, you knew a name by the name of Milan Andzic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He was a shopkeeper from Omarska and he owned a tavern called Trijaz; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also knew of a man by the name of Nedjo Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Nedjo Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This was a man who owned two restaurants, is that correct, the Europe restaurant, one in Prijedor, and one in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this Milan Andzic, he formed a paramilitary group, didn't he, that was led or commanded by a man named Radanovic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He financed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this Nenad Radanovic had been a taxi driver; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Nenad Radanovic also known as Cigo.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you said Mr. Andzic had financed this paramilitary group. By that do you mean that he provided uniforms and weapons and training, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he funded it. He provided the funds, the pay and he also purchased American uniforms for them, somewhere in Germany, through some contacts of his. And as for the weapons, this unit was armed by the Yugoslav Army, and they went through training in Manjaca, and Podkradica [phoen] and somewhere in the Banja Luka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And before the outbreak of war in Bosnia, this units was fighting in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They were established in Omarska, and they went through training under the control of the Yugoslav Army, and then they were sent to the front lines in Western Slavonia, to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the men who were in this paramilitary unit were local men from Omarska and Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, they were from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And when they returned to Prijedor from Croatia, they had a large amount of war booty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A large amount of war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And this was handed over to Mr. Andzic, and he collected this war booty and made profits from it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of the items that had been stolen and taken by this unit, by the members who fought in Western Slavonia was brought over and put in the warehouse, the owner of which was Milan Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Would it be possible to lower the arm of the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems okay now. We can manage this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you can move closer to the microphone now that we don't have to play peek-a-boo. Okay. So we are talking about the paramilitary formation. When this -- the one that Andzic formed, when the war broke out in Bosnia these same paramilitaries were the ones committing crimes and looting to a large extent in Prijedor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way. That unit was under the direct control of the 374th Motorised Brigade and the 43rd Motorised Brigade, under the command of Radmilo Zeljaja. They were, in other words, under the command of the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And were they -- they were looting and bringing goods back to Mr. Andzic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And they had participated in the attack on Kozarac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Together with the 5th Kozara Brigade led by Pero Covic. Their axis of attack on a Prijedor was Omarska, Kevjani, Jakupovici, Kamnecani [phoen], and Kozarac. Would you please just correct the transcript. It should read Pero Colic, C-o-l-i-c. That's right, that's correct now.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the same Mr. Andzic that we have been talking about, he was one of the people who financed and organised the establishment of Omarska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The Omarska camp as well as all of the other camps in Prijedor were established by the civilian authorities of the municipality of Prijedor. Milan Andzic provided logistics, since he is an Omarska resident. He also provided finances to secure food for the detainees. He also financed a Red Cross department which was in Omarska, which supposedly was to take care of the food that was to be given to the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And along with this Mr. Andzic, the other man we mentioned, Mr. Delic, also was behind the establishment of Omarska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They logistically aided those camps. But to reiterate, the Prijedor camps were established following a decision of the civilian authorities of the Prijedor municipality. These two men simply supported those camps, since they were well off.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the civilian authority you're referring to is the Prijedor Crisis Staff; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian authorities headed by the Crisis Staff of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. In the Brdjanin trial, and the reference there is page 12799, that's 1D04-2107, you testified that prior to the 30th of April, 1992, prior to that date, all incidents in Prijedor were committed by members of the Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also testified that after April 30th, 1992, paramilitary formations and gangs headed by people like Zigic and Dosan became active in Prijedor municipality and they took justice into their own hands; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sivac. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and I appear on behalf of Stojan Zupljanin. I'll have some questions for you today. Just a word of caution, since you have already testified here before, I want to remind you that since we use the same language, we should observe a pause between questions and answers. I can see that you speak quite fast, which is also my case. We should take care of that so that the other participants in the trial could follow. Mr. Sivac, the first question. In your previous testimony, you mentioned that you stopped working for the State Security Service in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Not state security. That's -- this was the security service and that was on the 1st of January, 1991 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which department? What did you work for? Was it the National Security Service or the DB that we used to call in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I worked in the encryption department of the centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the public security station?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. In the SUP of Prijedor. In 1990, it bore that title, the Secretariat of Internal Affairs. And within the secretariat, there was public security as well as the police, and a general administration service. In Prijedor, there was a branch office of the state security though. The centre of state security -- of the State Security Service was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you worked in the general sector or in the branch office?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. In the general sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, one moment, please. Mr. Witness, you said you worked in the security service until the 1st of January of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It was 1991 in the -- in the record. So it is 1990. 1st of January 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You worked in the communications and encryption department in the SUP of Prijedor. That is to say the Municipal Secretariat of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This was the schematic of organisation of such bodies in the former Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Following that did you remain as a reserve member? Did you remain with the reserve police in -- in -- during the war at all?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I was not assigned to any body or unit. I started working as a correspondent for the Sarajevo TV in Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Bosanski Dubica, Sanski Most, and I also covered parts of Croatia, neighbouring Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in your previous testimony, when you mentioned some other people working for the security service, you did not distinguish between those in the State Security Service and in the other type. You all referred to them as security employees; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We needed to clarify this, because in your previous testimony the terms we found were the state security and the security service.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I'll now go back to what my learned friend, Mr. Prosecutor, asked you just before the break. He invited you to identify Stojan Zupljanin in the courtroom. Let me ask you this: do you recall what Stojan Zupljanin looked like in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I can recall what he looked like more or less. He a bit more hair. He was greying at the time. And in Omarska, I mainly focussed on the political delegation. I mentioned the police delegation only in the margins. Zeljko Meakic and Simo Drljaca are the people I referred to because they were in charge of the Omarska camp. I did not refer to Mr. Zupljanin because he was part of the political delegation from Banja Luka. I focussed only on the people from the police delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may intervene, Mr. Krgovic. Inasmuch as this, quote/unquote, identification of Mr. Zupljanin seemed to have been taken up by both sides, Mr. Witness, did you know Mr. Zupljanin before that time, when -- when you saw him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not personally. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I should have asked, did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew he was chief of the security centre in Banja Luka. I didn't know him personally though. When I was still with the service, I don't remember having met him, ever, in the course of my duties. When the political delegation from Banja Luka arrived though, save for a great number of Banja Luka journalists, there was also Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, who was dressed in a camouflage blue and white police uniform and he also sported a dark blue beret. He escorted the political delegation from Banja Luka. After a short report by Zeljko Mejakic, who was the Omarska camp commander to Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Behind Zeljko Mejakic, there was Simo Drljaca who was the security chief from Prijedor, and Mr. Jankovic who was the police commander. When the ceremony was over and the report was given, as well as the salute, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, as well as Mr. Simo Drljaca, met, and together with the other members of the delegation, they toured the Omarska camp. From that place, they went through the detainee lineup and went straight for the management building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on a minute. Mr. Sivac, were you able, at that occasion, to identify right away, Mr. Zupljanin; or did someone else tell you at that occasion, that this was Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. It took only a brief moment for someone to be identified in such a delegation. It could only have been Stojan Zupljanin. There were no problems regarding identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But just how did you then manage to identify Mr. Zupljanin without knowing him in advance? Which -- on which basis did you conclude that this was, indeed, Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on his previous TV appearances, when Mr. Stojan Zupljanin provided interviews. I can't recall exactly, but I think it had to do with an operation carried out by the centre of the security service in Kotor Varos municipality when part of that municipality was ethnically cleansed. He appeared before TV cameras and explained why that operation took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand it correctly, you were then able, on that basis, to recognise the person as being Mr. Zupljanin, when you saw him live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As well as the other people who stood next to me, my mates from the camp, they covered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, very briefly just to touch on that, I would just refer back also to his direct examination, page 24, lines 23, which also covers that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, you just said that you saw Stojan Zupljanin following that operation in Kotor Varos. This apparently took place before you were arrested and taken to Omarska and that is the basis of how you recognised him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What if I told that you the Kotor Varos operation and the conflict which erupted there happened in mid-June and early July 1991, and that it was not on the basis --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was not and on that basis that you would recognise him what would you say?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been regarding some other operation, but I know fully well that Mr. Stojan Zupljanin gave interviews and it was only then that I realised who he was and what he -- his job was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before you were arrested, did you know that there were no operations in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did mention Kotor Varos but I saw some other interviews alongside the interview on the occasion of that operation. It is possible though that those interviews took place when I was still back in the apartment in Prijedor. I don't know whether the operation involved Sanski Most or something else. That's something I'm not certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were being proofed by the Prosecutor did they show you a photograph or a -- footage of Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Well, yes, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. There was a photograph with Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. He a beard and wore civilian clothes with a group of what seemed to be friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you testified in the Stakic case, as well as in the previous statement you gave to the Prosecutors, you said it was Vojo Kupresanin. In actual fact you mixed the two people.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I spoke in haste, and I later on corrected myself and I still stand by when I say that build Mr. Zupljanin was in Omarska in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw him in Omarska did very a beard?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, when you came to testify in the Stakic case you said it was Vojo Kupresanin. That is not in dispute, correct? Let's go step by step; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I may have misspoken, since I speak fast. I may have said Vojo Kupresanin in some context. But I recall well that a delegation included Predrag Radic who was the chief from Banja Luka. But it is beyond dispute that the main person was Radoslav Brdjanin on that day and I focussed on him. He was the most interesting person there, because he was the man number one of the Serb Autonomous District or the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, when you testified in the Stakic case, that afternoon when you arrived, the Prosecutor showed you a number of articles from Kozarski Vjesnik which you had not seen before that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That is it possible although I did not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction. It's page 44, line 24, and then answer on line 25. I think maybe it is a some small typo or error. I think the answer should be related to the question, actually. The end of the question, and the answer was that what -- what Mr. Sivac said that Mr. Zupljanin did not wear a beard at that time. It's a bit confusing, so maybe we could clarify that, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, I apologise for this. We probably spoke fast, both you and I. But my question was whether Mr. Zupljanin, at the time, had a beard, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he did not have a moustache either.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A lot of time has elapsed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1378 now. Could we just zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We see this article before us, and you were shown this article in the Stakic case, and you had said then that it had been shown to you just before the trial. And do you recall actually being shown this and reading it?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here it is mentioned that Stojan Zupljanin was a member of that delegation.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you obtained this information at the Stakic trial?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then, in the Brdjanin cases, on the basis of this article, you changed your testimony and you said that this man was in fact Stojan Zupljanin. That helped you refresh your memory, right?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. But after I read there article that I was 100 per cent sure that it was, indeed, Stojan Zupljanin and that this article, too, proves that I was correct when I identified him as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the correction in -- in the testimony came as a result of this article as well, where there was mention that it was Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
