utterances.text: Well, no, but it was -- it was my first impression that it was in fact Zupljanin, but it is possible that I misspoke and that I just mentioned the other name by error.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And frequently in your testimony, you actually substituted and kept confusing the names, Zupljanin and Kupresanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it is possible but I don't see that there is any big problem with that because Stojan Zupljanin was, in my view, a bit similar to Kupresanin. He looked a bit like him. They were good-looking men, remarkable features.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Vojo Kupresanin was blond wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. He actually had highlights, blond or grey highlights and I'm not sure whether it was natural because I'm not a hairdresser, but that's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you thought that Vojo Kupresanin, too, was a person who came to Prijedor to implement this separation in MUP along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not see Kupresanin at the time. But I know for sure that Zupljanin was in that delegation, because the Banja Luka media, which were under the direct control of the Serbian Democratic Party, actually published on the very following day and mentioned that Stojan Zupljanin, among others, was a member of this delegation that was sent because, according to them, there was some kind of an assassination attempt plotted, being plotted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you actually published a book about these events surrounding Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. And I failed to mention this to the Trial Chamber. Currently I'm a freelance analyst and writer, and I am very interested in the events in Prijedor over the past 20 years. And in two years, it will have been 20 years since the ethnic cleansing in Prijedor, and I am trying to write a book - I'm also done with it - where the truth about Prijedor will be told, and the name -- the title of the book will be; the Serbian Lies and Deceptions and the Truth about Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you wrote a book entitled: How big is the Carsija in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness replied with a yes, but it was not recorded in the transcript. Could we now pull up in e-court 2D09- --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Sivac your answer did not find its way into transcript. When I asked you about the book entitled: How Big is Carsija in Prijedor. That's the book that that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I wrote that book, I think, in 1993, after I left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we now have 2D09-0331, please. Your Honours, this is a book authored by the witness. It was downloaded into e-court, but it hasn't been translated because the Defence did not have the intention of using this book until we received -- the proofing notes from the Prosecutor and we realised that we would need to verify or clarify a couple of things and I will only be referring to two or three pages. I will ask the witness to read it and I will only ask him about that portion. We have submitted a request for translation. However, because we received the information from the Prosecutor rather late, we were unable to provide the translation in a timely fashion. Could we please show the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, this is the book we were discussing; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This book was prepared on the basis of a large number of newspaper reports that I wrote about the Prijedor events. My colleagues actually collected them, compiled them, and issued it as -- and printed it as a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please pull up page ERN 00124083.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 01124083, page 63 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 086083. We need 083; this is 086. 24083.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please take a look at the first part of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we need the previous page. 083.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this book that you published in 1993, as you said, in the last paragraph of this first part it says: "From Banja Luka..." Could you please read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: "From Banja Luka, Vujo Kupresanin came in person. He was a teacher. And one of the leading Serbs in Bosanski Krajina in order to talk the police in Prijedor into a division within their ranks. In that, he was not successful as it seems."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you wrote this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what source you based this on?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, all the information that we had, we received from the journalists from Banja Luka, our colleagues. As for us, we were banned. We were not allowed to work, especially me, and as of March 1992, I stopped reporting, and I only informed my headquarters and reported to them the main events. We were unable to provide any video footage to the Sarajevo television, and as for the Banja Luka studio you should know that it had already been taken over by the Serbian Democratic Party and they had started broadcast the programmes of the Serbian television from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the information on the events on Prijedor that Vojo Kupresanin was in Prijedor, you received that information from Banja Luka, right, not from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, from my colleagues in Banja Luka, who were close to the circles of the Serbian leadership in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall perhaps the names of the people who provided this information to you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, the information was provided by our colleagues, Slobodan Pesevic, Boro Maric, Kozomara.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about this particular bit of information?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically, but I received this from Mr. Boro Grubic who was in direct contact with colleagues from Banja Luka because they trusted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the arrival of Stojan Zupljanin in April 1992, you said that the same information was provided to you by Boro Grubic, you received that information from him?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a colleague of mine. He was the editor, and he was in the group, League for Peace, that actually rallied, that conducted rallies outside the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you were not part of this rally when they went out, outside the municipal building, when the representatives of the League arrived?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not see any members of that delegation, did you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, precisely because they wanted to avoid any kind of verbal incidents. The delegation was brought into the building from the back entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you must be aware that Mr. Brdjanin was not in that delegation, that it was only Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Bajazid Jahic, who was Mr. Zupljanin's deputy, two policeman; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. The information we received was that the delegation, among whom was Stojan Zupljanin, was in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't know who else was there with Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Maybe I mentioned Radoslav Brdjanin, because he was the boss there, and I think without the political leaders, such a thing would not have been possible. It would not be possible to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And at this time, outside the municipal building a group of people gathered. You said members of the Patriotic League and they had Green Berets and lilies as insignia, correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not correct. These were just regular people. How could it be the way you are putting. The people who were in the rally were Croats and Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose thereafter meeting was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that they had come to negotiate the division of the Prijedor police by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that following that, the delegation, a member of which Mr. Stojan Zupljanin was, went to have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request, could the counsel please repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know after this event because they were displeased with the fact that this delegation actually was sneaked into the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will repeat my question. So my question was, and this was not recorded in the transcript. My question was: whether you know that after this, the delegation -- or, rather, Stojan Zupljanin and the other person who was with him that they went to the polices station in Prijedor to have a meeting there with Mr. Talundzic and that they spent some five hours there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. All I know is that the group that had protested, because of the division of the police, very soon dispersed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My question was not in there, I'm looking at the transcript. I was perhaps speeding, as it were. So my question was that Stojan Zupljanin, together with other men who was -- who were in the delegation with him, went to the police station in Prijedor to meet Mr. Talundzic. Do you know who Mr. Talundzic was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the public security station there Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Would you like me to tell you more about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, just his position.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of the public security station, a member of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting that was held in the municipal building, do you know that, in addition to Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Jahic the meeting was attended Mr. Mirza Mujadzic and Mr. Muhamed Cehajic, the municipal president?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that in my earlier testimonies that this meeting was attended also by members of the then-authorities in Prijedor, and the president of the municipality at the time was the legally elected professor, Muhamed Cehajic, and Dr. Mirza Mujadzic, probably as a member of the Party for Democratic Action, also attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you know that the purpose or the subject that was discussed at the meeting was to actually appease the situation in Prijedor until a political solution was found, including the situation in MUP, this meeting being in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. All we knew was that the delegation had arrived Prijedor and that they came to force the then-authorities in Prijedor to divide the Prijedor police and we had very little information because this was a closed meeting, and I'm telling you only about what we were told at that time, in reply to our question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that one of the results of those talks which included Mr. Zupljanin was that when it comes to the Prijedor police that there were no changes to be made to the personnel or the insignia. This included all personnel, those who signed and those who did not sign this oath to the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Do you mean the April or the May meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The April/May -- or the April meeting.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know what the conclusion was, but I know that by April the professional policemen of the SUP of Prijedor already sported the Serbian insignia with the four S's. If you want me to, I can specify the names of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 2D18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just one second, please. Mr. Witness, could you repeat the title of your book, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title of my book is: "How big is the Carsija in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we believe the meaning of it is the public opinion or as the rumour has it in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to translate. It's a verse from a Bosnian folk epic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But we have some description of what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, have a look at the document. It was sent by Stojan Zupljanin to all public security stations. You used to work for the police and I believe you recognise an incoming telegram?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the signing of statements and the insignia of the Serbian MUP. Have a look at the fourth paragraph from the top which says: "The obligations mentioned in this telegram do not apply to the Prijedor and Kotor Varos SUPs. Authorised officials at these stations may continue to wear the current insignia if they wish to do so until further notice (until the political situation in these municipalities is resolved)." Mr. Sivac, this document illustrates the very thing I mentioned to you and that is that Mr. Zupljanin's visit, as well as that of Mr. Jakic was in this vein, in trying to reach a political solution and the conclusion was not to change any insignia in Prijedor and not to have any divisions there. Was that the information you received?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, in the end, we received information to the effect that the Prijedor police was not to be split until further notice. That was in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about having heard of Mr. Zupljanin's visits to Prijedor after that, and that again loyalty oaths were being mentioned and how Muslim employees were to acknowledge the existence of the Serbian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do seem to recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said you heard that over the radio.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. My colleague, Mr. Grubic tried to join the meeting at the Ljubija iron ore mine which is vis-a-vis the SUP building. However he was not allowed, since it was a closed meeting with the employees of the security service. From certain people from the security service with whom he was on good terms, he received that type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, is it possible that you mixed up two meetings in April? One which held in the municipal building, which then continued in the police station building; and that you mixed up the two meetings in April, having concluded that some of them spilled over into May which were attended by Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. On the 30th of April, as you know, there was a pouch carried out by the military and the police. There was a takeover of power -- of power in Prijedor, and the police was unified at that time. On the 30th of April, the Serb colleagues in the police station in Prijedor disarmed all Muslim and Croat colleagues who happened to have been there. They took away their weapons and took over the Security Service Centre in Prijedor. After that, at the meeting which was called, a decision was made that the employees of the security service who were not Serbs, i.e. Muslims and Croats, should sign loyalty oaths if they wanted to remain in their positions. They were required to do so in order to show their loyalty to the new Serb authorities. A colleague of mine who had worked with me for a number of years in the communications and encryption department was the only Muslim remaining in the centre, and after that meeting, he talked to me, asking me whether he should sign the loyalty oath or not because he was undecided. I told him, Well, think carefully and decide for yourself what to do so. He did sign eventually. Nonetheless, he was soon kicked out. As for the rest, by late May, were taken to Keraterm and Omarska and killed there. Out of the total number of professional policeman and employees of the security service, less than five remain alive. Their only mistake was that they were Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So Bozo Grubic provided you information with this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Bozo Grubic was in the iron ore mine building. However he was denied access to the meeting. And from Mirsad Cahuric, who worked with me in the encryption department, I also learned similar information. He, however, was witness to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not hear that over the radio, sometime in May 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, one could hear all sorts of things on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But not this?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. This came directly from the participants or people who were asked to sign loyalty oaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the Kozarac meeting. You could not hear that over Radio Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's a different thing. Do not mix the two. Do not mix the meeting about loyalty oaths and Kozarac where the police was forced, although 95 per cent of them were Muslim, to accept the new insignia and be loyal to the new Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you not say that that meeting was held in Prijedor in the iron ore mine and that there was a rally in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. You are confusing the two or trying to confuse me. There were no Green Berets in front of the municipal building. These were regular people, mostly intellectuals, headed by Dr. Eso Sadikovic, and it was decided at that meeting that the Prijedor police not be split up. And as I said, the delegation entered the municipal building through the back door. The second meeting was after it's 30th of April, after the military police takeover took place, when they took over the police, the municipality building and the radio station. By that time, there was already an ultimatum in place, either you sign a loyalty oath or you go. Either way, your fate was going to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Kozarac meeting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's a third thing. It was a sealed-off area. The new Serb authorities sealed it off, cut electricity, water, telephone lines and Kozarac was surrounded by arsenals of weapon, tank units, artillery, and they all waited for the right moment to start of the ethnic cleansing of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the meeting in Kozarac. Where did that information come from about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, to repeat, we got that information from our Banja Luka colleagues. It's a delegation from Banja Luka attempted to get in touch with the political leadership in Kozarac to force them to surrenderer and to acknowledge the new Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's when the Green Berets appeared in Kozarac, protesting in front of the building where the meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: There were no Green Berets in Kozarac. The police was there. What context do you put these Green Berets in? You seem to be quite obsessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is you who is obsessed, rather than me, and I can show you your book, which is 2D09-0331.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your book, the ERN number is 01124109. The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please read out loud the paragraph starting with: "It is because of that, from Banja Luka ..."

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The third from the top.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the witness please be asked to read slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was because of that, that" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking that you read slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "It was because of that, that the chief of the security services centre, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, urgently arrived from Banja Luka with his escort so that with the help of Simo Drljaca, Simo Miskovic and others of the city council of the SDS, they should try to convince and persuade the people of Kozarac to acknowledge the Serb authorities and to sign loyalty oaths to it. The people of Kozarac did not budge. The response was clear. This time as well they would not consent to any preconditions acknowledging the forcible takeover, and they would refuse to sport any Serbian insignia in Carsija. That is, the old town. They only acknowledged the legally elected authorities and the sovereign independent republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Around the building where the talks were being held there was a spontaneous gathering of a larger group of residents. A few young men sported red berets with lilies on their heads. It was a clear answer to the creators of the new order in this area that should go back home with job undone. Back to the most Chetnik town of all, Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It seem there is was a mistake. Not Red Berets. I think you said Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: "There were a few young men who had green berets with lilies, only a few."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we are at the time for a break. Is this a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, you've read this portion of your book. Do you recall writing that down in the book, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Which part are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the previous part. Let go back a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I do recall, the portion that I mentioned that in the group that had gathered outside the police station there were several young men with green berets on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely. That's why I wanted to take you back there. Tell me, Mr. Sivac, the source for this information was again the same journalist, Mr. Grubic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. No, sir. Kozarac at that time was tightly sealed off from the rest of the word. Writing this book in 1993, I came by some photographs from some people were in Kosovo, photographs taken in Kozarac at the time. And one of the photos depicted a group of policemen from Kozarac whom I knew and a group of men that I did not know, who were not familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned that in your book; correct? You did write this in your book?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did say there were just a few people with green berets in that group, and at that time that was a sort of symbol for those people who were fighting for a democratic Bosnia which, at the time was already internationally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these two bits of information, the meeting at Kozarac and the meeting at the mine, this is information that you did not get from Prijedor. You got it from Mr. Grubic and the second bit of information from people from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. I got it from the people from Banja Luka, a group of journalists from Banja Luka, because the -- the -- the group of people who were accompanying the delegation or who came to Omarska, they provided that information to us. And because Kozarac was shut off from the rest of the world we were frequently on the phones with our colleagues from Banja Luka, who provided a large number of information about the activities of the leadership of the Serbian Autonomous Krajina as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these two bits of information did you not hear them on the radio you got them from the sources that just mentioned a few moments ago; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Not on Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, let me ask you, or, rather, the reason that I'm asking this is in the proofing notes where you were proofed by the Prosecution, you said something to the effect that you received this information from Radio Prijedor. So quite the contrary to what are you saying now.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that I said that then, but the main source of information came from Banja Luka. In other words, I received that information from Banja Luka. It is possible that Radio Prijedor broadcast that information because they broadcast everything, but the most reliable information came from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So where you said to the Prosecutor about the source of information for those two meetings that is not correct. What is correct is what you are saying here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that if the Prosecutor asked me where I obtained that information from, it's possible that I said that maybe I got it from Radio Prijedor, but as I recalled all these events after that conversation with him, I recall the sources of information that we received at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it seems, because this is something that you said to the Prosecutor yesterday, you cannot tell us with full certainty where you actually obtained this information from; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, let's put it that way. It was either from Banja Luka or from Radio Prijedor. But, in any case, that information did reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you're not certain of the provenance of this particular bit of information.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, right now, I'm pretty certain that it did come from the Banja Luka circle of journalists, and Radio Prijedor probably broadcast that, because they broadcast more or less everything. But they, too, could not get -- could not have gotten this information from the spot where the meeting was actually held. They, too, received that information from the same source why we got it from, from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But didn't you say just a few minutes ago that the information that you got on the meeting in the mine, that you received that information from some people who were not allowed to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, for that particular bit of information, yes, that's what I said. That has nothing to do with this bit of information. I have -- I keep thinking that what you're referring to is the meeting, the conversation at the police building, where they were trying to actually make these people accept the takeover and the division within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was asking you about the meeting at the mine.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, at the mine, as I've already said, and I'm quite certain about that, because this was closed meeting, it was closed for the public and closed for journalists, my colleague Grubic who used his informers at the security service, he was nearby. He was near the area where the meeting was held and after the meeting he received this information, and then he also obtained direct information about what was being discussed at these meetings. And as for me, I received the direct information from Mr. Mirsad Cahuric who attended that meeting. He was in the Communications Department of the police and that's where I knew him from. The meeting where the gentlemen from Banja Luka and the gentlemen from Prijedor were actually discussing on the mode of work of the Banja Luka police and then someone asked about what about those people who had not been expelled from their jobs -- Muslim or ethnic or Croatian ethnicities, and then they were told that such people should be made to sign their oath of loyalty to the new Serbian authorities and Mr. Simo Drljaca agreed to that, so that is a number of people who worked at the security station signed the oath of loyalty but another number of men did not. But even those who did sign it ended up in Omarska and Keraterm and that's where life -- where their lives ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, the meeting that you mentioned, the police meeting, was the information you had about was neither from the Banja Luka journalists nor from Radio Prijedor, but, rather, Boro Grubic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that too. But I think that this was also reported on Radio Prijedor and I also think there was an article that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik, but I'm not sure exactly when that was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, so all the information you received or all information that came either from Banja Luka or from Prijedor, they were actually reported on Radio Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for instance, if Mr. Zupljanin came and attended a meeting there, it would certainly have been printed in the Kozarski Vjesnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, but that depended on the editors of Kozarski Vjesnik. I never was one, so I don't think you should put that question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But, for instance, if Mr. Zupljanin came and attended the meeting this would certainly have been reported, correct, in the Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, again all I can say is that I was not an editor there and I can only say that they were -- they used, for the most part, the news agency's reports or news, but how exactly it was that they came by information that they printed in Kozarski Vjesnik, I really don't know exactly and I never really tried to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask you, is Boro Grubic alive?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, he passed away a few years ago and he was a very good friend of mine. We worked together for some seven or eight years. He worked as a journalist in Oslobodjenje and I worked on the television in Bosnia, and we actually helped each other out with our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So there is no one who is alive today who could confirm what you said here about these two meetings, the one at the municipal building and the one at the mine?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: I did not look for whether anyone was alive or not today, but that is the result or the consequence of most of these people having been killed at the camps. Also, they're of the age when death is not so far away, and in any case, I'm very sorry about Mr. Boro Grubic. He was a very good friend of mine and a close associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he was a guard in Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. At first, let me just elaborate a bit. At first, Mr. Boro Grubic was a member of the Patriotic League and he was against any ethnic divisions in Prijedor; however, when some politicians, Serb politicians, put pressure on him, he had to accept what was offered and he even accepted being a guard at Trnopolje for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please take a look at 65 -- P1378, actually. Exhibit P1378. This is an article -- it isn't easy for anyone; that's the title of the article. Could you please tell me this. You said in answer to my question in a Banja Luka paper you read something about an alleged assassination attempt on Mr. Zupljanin's life?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I think I recall that. It was reported in the Banja Luka press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you recognised Stojan Zupljanin because he gave some interviews about events in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not explicitly mention Kotor Varos. I said that I remembered his statements on television at that time and earlier when he talked about the general security situation in the Serbian Bosanski Krajina and the problems that they were facing and so on. But specifically the first time that I saw him on television, I can't really say when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, please take a look at this article and then at the bottom you will see where mention is made of the people who visited Prijedor and the portion where Stojan Zupljanin's name is mentioned. It says: Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of the Banja Luka CSB, who an earlier time by a group of 500 Muslim extremists, led by Hamid Ergovic [phoen], Asif Kapetanovic, [indiscernible], Mirzad Mujadzic, and other extremists from Prijedor, prepared a fiery welcome. Now, is the source of information that you had for that assassination attempt this particular article?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. I think I read about this in Srpski Glas, that was the name of the paper. That's a Banja Luka paper and it was published there, but I think it was also broadcast on Serbian television as a news item.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at the second column at the bottom. It says: "Because of a misconception that they had accepted the Serbian state and the Krajina AR, 55 of our men in Kotor Varos were killed and the Green Berets from Vecici were proud that they were the ones who killed Stevilovics [phoen]." Now isn't what you said about Mr. Zupljanin, isn't that based on this article that you had occasion to read?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. Let me explain. It was not like that. It was based on a news report and the statements made by Mr. Zupljanin on Serbian television at the time. And if you wish, you can ask for this video footage from the archives of the Banja Luka television. I'm sure they have a lot of that footage in their archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, let me complete this part of my examination. When you were in Prijedor, before you were arrested, you had never seen Mr. Stojan Zupljanin in these -- at these places where you say you did?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I did not see him myself. Not in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Nor did you see -- nor did you personally see any of the other men that you mentioned here that they were there allegedly?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Which people did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Simo Brdjanin, Vukic, I'm talking about the April/May events?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I met Simo Drljaca on a daily basis. He was a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm referring to the meetings that you described, did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, not at the meetings because we were not allowed to attend these meetings. These were closed-type meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I will have to repeat my question and I will slow down. So, I am asking you about these three meetings that you mentioned earlier. In other words, the meeting at Prijedor municipal building, the Ljubija mine in Prijedor, and the meeting at Kozarac. You did -- you personally did not see any of the participants of those meetings at the time when those meeting were held; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, the first meeting was almost an underground type of meeting because the -- the one at the municipal building. It was very confidential. The second meeting was also confidential. And the third meeting where we received information from our colleagues that the political delegation from Banja Luka and Mr. Zupljanin went to Kozarac to try to convince the police and the political leadership in Kozarac to acknowledge and accept the situation and the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, excuse me for interrupting, but my question referred to specifically -- it was a simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do not overlap. And as you see on the screen, the court reporter is asking that you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, I apologise. Can you please just answer my question and when you and I talk at the same time, when we overlap, then the record does not clearly show what is a question and what is the answer. So could you please try to answer -- to be as brief as possible in your answers, just answer with yes or no, if you can. So all the three meetings that we mentioned, you personally did not see either Stojan Zupljanin or any of the other individual who are said to have attended those meetings. You did not see any of them personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That's correct, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you have no first-hand information about the actual attendees of those meetings. You only actually learned of that later on from the sources that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The information that we obtained from the sources that we used for our newspaper reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am finished with this topic. Let me ask you something about the events which came about after the 30th of April, 1992. In your previous testimony in the Stakic case, you mentioned an event which you called an attempt to liberate or an attack on Prijedor of the 29th of May, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It took place early in the morning, when a unit led by Slavko Acimovic tried to take over Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was no unit. It was a group of Prijedor residents who had to leave their homes in the first wave after the Serb takeover, because they refused to respond to a call-up, to go and wage war in Croatia. Immediately after the 30th of April, when the Serbs took over power in Prijedor, the first to be targeted were such people. Explosive devices were thrown on their houses, and those people simply had to get away from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they attempted to take back Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm sorry, and I apologise to the Judges, but this would require much elaboration. In my research work, I concluded this. Everything that had to do with this so-called occupation of Prijedor, as Serbs would have it, and I call it the liberation of Prijedor, was a masquerade. It was prearranged in the Prijedor barracks where there were certain military intelligence officers who had simply arranged with a group of people from the Slavko Acimovic group for it to be done, to have an alibi, to have a reason to ethnically cleans Prijedor and establish camps. It was all prearranged. I have documents to prove that and I hope that in the subsequent proceedings I would be able to put forth for this Tribunal to be able to see the means used by the Serb authorities in Prijedor. That is why precisely, precisely why, I'm writing this book called: Serb falsification or how to counterfeit history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the book you referred to, you describe in detail the structure of the units led by Slavko Acimovic. You explain in detail the axes of attack, the types of weapons and events surrounding the liberation attempt in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I received that information from people who directly participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You were also able to observe parts of that operation from your window in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I could see parts of it from my apartment in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you certainly know that the plan was to destroy the large gasoline terminal in Brezicanin and to destroy an overpass and a bridge over a nearby river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No. You are misquoting, Mr. Krgovic. When I discussed this with the people from this group who were forced to assemble in a certain part of Prijedor municipality, they told me that their intentions at first were to try and breakthrough to Bihac and the Bihac area, which was under B and H army control, and to also potentially try to launch a number of smaller diversions, in order to retaliate against the Serbs for the things they had done in Prijedor. I also said a moment ago that in the Prijedor barracks there had been a morbid plan prepared for the group from Kurevo to be brought at any cost into Prijedor for it to be destroyed and, indeed, it was so. In that group, they had a few of their own men, a few moles who is had come to the Prijedor barracks, from Radmilo Zeljaja, Radovan Jajic and others, including Simo Drljaca, they were informed and briefed on how and what to do in Prijedor in order to follow it up with the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor and destruction of property, as well as rounding up people to be taken to camps. They only needed an excuse which was provided by the group's incursion into Prijedor. It was all arranged with some people from Slavko Acimovic's group. A deal was struck between them and some officers in the Prijedor barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your book you quote a friend of yours who explained these events to you. You called this part of the book: Fighter Mirzad's diary. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you describe the composition of that unit, you refer to four groups. The first group was in the area of Ljubija, headed by Kemal Alagic and Captain Sead Halilovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The second group, in Zegar Polje [phoen] and Tukovo, headed by Slavko Acimovic. That's the person we have been referring to; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A third group in the area of Rizvanovici, Hambarine, Biscani led by Lieutenant Muhic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fourth group in the area of Skela, Raskovac, Puharska headed by Mesic, as well as Hadzija, and Nenad Babic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The plan was -- well, Mesic went to Prijedor and agreed with the residents of Puharska that once the group is inside Prijedor attacking certain facilities that 500 men would join them from Puharska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That was agreed. However this was just a farce, as I said already, for Slavko and other groups to have an excuses to go into Prijedor. Izmet Mehic, Hadzija, was a Trojan horse in that operation. He was the person who had met with Simo Drjlaca, Radmilo Zeljaja and Radovan Arsic met in the Prijedor barracks. He arranged that Slavko Acimovic and his group be led towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992, Slavko Acimovic's group split into several groups and took different routes. The first group went towards the football stadium going through Sredice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 1P015266 to the witness. P015266.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript, it should be Slavko Ecimovic rather that Slavko Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was introduced by the Prosecutor. It's a map. It's P015266. I hope I'm quoting it correctly from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this please be corrected. It is it Ecimovic not Acimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think the counsel is actually adding an extra number. It should be five digits instead of six. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I believe it is P1526. I only know it is not double 6 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map of Prijedor. You have a marker. Please indicate the axes where this group crossed over the Sana, led by Babic. Can you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This group with Sadik Mehcic [phoen], where did it cross the Sana river at Sedice [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, this is a very low detail map. There is no river Sana, there but this is the general area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark that with a 1.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The second group, Muhic's group, that wept across the bridge to the municipality and the mine?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, there is no bridge here or the street which leads up to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What is the approximate route?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The only thing about Prijedor I have is the name of it. I would have to a detailed map of the town then could I mark it. This is completely inadequate. It would serve nothing but to confuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you only mark the axes where they started from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They all crossed the Sana, and there is another important thing I need to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If this is of any importance to your case, I suggest we find a better and a more detailed map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The one I have is also very poor, in terms of details. But -- well, let's me ask you this verbally, just for the sake of leaving us a background to the attack.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I would be more than happy to indicate it on the map, but I really can't use this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecutor has a more detailed map.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I have one in my hotel room. Had I known that these will be the questions, I would have brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do not mention that you have anything in your hotel room. Otherwise we will see you back in a less than a year.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be my destiny. I seem to have a finger in every pie. I just keep changing my suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a map which is part of Mr. Sivac's 92 ter package. The 65 ter number it's been given is 10446, and perhaps that may suit their purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have that exhibit. I think it is number 8 in the package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The first thing I asked you about, the group which crossed the Sana, next to the leather manufacturing facility.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's somewhere just following the Ada. Somewhere here. Yes. That's the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The second group, with Lieutenant Asim Muhnic [phoen] crossing the bridge at Berek?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is it, this arch here. There are two bridges, actually. One is here and the other on the other side. I think they went through the old town following this route towards the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they eventually reached the reserve officers' hall?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were aiming for the high school centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they reached the SUP and municipal building?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, from the back. They reached the museum which is to the side of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is the SUP. It says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Put a 3 there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the third group led by Kemal Divljak went across Visici Most eventually reaching the red sky-scraper.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the periphery of town. This is Lukavica and radio Prijedor. I think it is here somewhere. This is not the best map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Put a 4 there.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: They reached Lukavica. They never reached the radio station building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The group led by Slavko Ecimovic crossed the Visici Most and reached the Prijedor Hotel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the bridge and this is the Prijedor Hotel. That is number 5, I think, right next to the Sana river.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please put a 5 a bit below.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, the marker is a bit thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: They took up their positions and that's when the clash erupted. However, when the army started using heavy weaponry in a counter-attack attempt, they withdrew and the army were in front of the SUP and the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The attack lasted for about half an hour. Perhaps to reiterate for the Judges this had been rearranged from certain forward positions in the sky-scrapers in Prijedor, there were sniper shooters, sharpshooters on duty there, and the night before there event, all of them who could observe this part of town were withdrawn. There's even a written order by Simo Drljaca for them to be temporarily removed from their positions in order for this -- for these groups to go into town as far as possible so that the Serb army and police could destroy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The group headed by Slavko Ecimovic managed to destroy a position at Rebar and they set fire to the Prijedor Hotel?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but only the ground floor, the reception area. In the Prijedor Hotel, much before that, there were military police forces that had been brought in. The notorious Martic's Men, and they were accommodated in that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the group that had managed to get through to the underpass but they did not actually succeed in that because those 500 men from Puharska did not join them; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. Because two days earlier the Serbian television, and have I that newspaper article as well, reported where the people from Puharska and Kevljani and who were at barracks, they agreed to voluntarily surrender their weapons and the weapons that had been issued to them by the municipal Secretariat of Territorial Defence as well as the -- their own weapons that they had, meaning pistols and rifles, hunting rifles and so on, all of this was just a farce. This was just a way for Slavko and his men to be brought into Prijedor and destroyed. And then the tensions among the Serb population increased and they all started on their move on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion during this attack on the police station, a lot of people were killed there; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not correct. This was written in a way that would actually romanticise a bit the role of those people who had the courage to actually fight on that occasion. But I think there weren't so many killed, there were just a few people who got killed on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, as interesting all of this is from a historical point of view, I'm just a bit uncertain about the relevance to this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now move to the substance. In fact, because the witness talked about this in the Stakic case and he mentioned the events in Stari Grad and the shelling of Stari Grad, my intention was to put these two events into context, because this is an intro to the attack on Prijedor itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was no attack on Stari Grad by this group. They just passed through Stari Grad to reach those positions and then they withdrew across the Sana and into the woods. And as for the reprisals, I have already said that the Serbian authorities in Prijedor actually took advantage of this event and accused the Muslims of trying to massacre -- to commit a massacre in Prijedor as had happened during World War II in order to actually mobilise the Serb population, and on that morning all the Serbs actually appeared dressed in uniforms and armed and they were ready to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sivac, could you please show us where Prijedor is on this map?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite clearly show that part, the Stari Grad part, but it's approximately here in this area where I put the circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And is this where these men came from? That was the axis of attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no just one group. You mentioned the Kemal Divljak group, but Slavko Ecimovic reached the check-point at the bridge over Sana, and disarmed the people there and reached the hotel. So only Kemal Alagic Divljak's group actually went through the Stari Grad area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as they were withdrawing, they were withdrawing and fighting, they were shelled by the Serb forces and they withdrew across the river and into the woods; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. They crossed the Sana. Actually they were completely broken up. There was no general axis along a route which they withdrew. They were completely in disarray. They were in various parts of Prijedor, the parts towards the radio station, some -- some men were withdrawing that way. A part of the men were with withdrawing towards Nahija [phoen] downstream of Prijedor because the Serb artillery, around 5.00, began a fierce shelling from the airport and other elevations, the hills around the town, where the artillery had been positioned a few months earlier. They started their shelling of Stari Grad, Zagrad, portions of Skela for the most part the areas populated by Muslims for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the fiercest fighting on that morning were -- was in Partizanska Street and the Lukavica cafe; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's where a group headed by Mesic, Hadzija, who was the Trojan horse acting for Simo Drljaca and Radmilo Zeljaja. They arrived there and they barricaded themselves in that inn and then the specials, led by Zoran Karlica, a fighter from Slavonia, a very well-known local man from Prijedor arrived there and he dispersed or destroyed the group of -- this group in the inn and they captured Slavko Ecimovic alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this Mesic, Izet, was killed on that occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I have statements that were compiled by the Serb state security after these events where the people who had killed Izet Mesic, Hadzija, said that he had told them that he had carried out his task and that he should be taken to the barracks to see Zeljaja. However, they did not believe him. They did not believe that this was a prearranged deal, that it was part of their agreement and they killed him on the spot. And as for Slavko Ecimovic, he was captured alive, and he was later assassinated in Omarska camp. And in reprisal for this, his neighbours, Serbs who were all armed went to his home where they killed his mother, father, brother, sister-in-law. And, to this day, these people are free and they freely walk around Prijedor and no one was brought to justice for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these groups in disarray they were going back the same way across the Sana, right, they were returning the same way?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. There was a general disarray. As I said, they were just trying to get away and cross the river Sava. And as for the other group, they were along the -- they went -- they tried to withdraw along the left bank of the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you saw Serb tanks opening fire on them while they were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no I saw artillery pieces and cannon that were positioned in the vicinity of my own house. They were opening fire on Stari Grad, the old part of town, and the Muslim parts of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that where the attackers were coming from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no. There were no more attackers. They were active some hour, hour and a half in Prijedor and then they were broken up and they withdrew to the other side of the river. There were no more attackers. Do you understand, Mr. Krgovic? This is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I'm just asking you about their axis of operation. Was the fire opened on those axes where the attackers had been advancing from?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, no, they opened fire on parts of the town that had nothing to do with these attackers. The only thing was that these areas were settled -- the people living there were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us those parts of town?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Stari Grad was completely deployed. A 400-year-old part of town, some houses there were completely destroyed. First there was looting, and then they were shelled and then they were torched and finally destroyed. So this portion here, the part called Zagrad on the left bank of the Berika rivulet and parts of Partizanska Street were under attack by the Serb artillery and the Serb army. On the second day, they began with a wholesale destruction of historic and religious monuments in Prijedor in old town and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about this. Whether you agree with me when talking about the areas that the Serb artillery opened fire. This was actually those areas where the attack had come from; correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no that is not correct. They only used that part, the Stari Grad part of Prijedor to pass through there. They did not engage the enemy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the Serb artillery and the Serb fire was opened on the areas through which they actually moved and tried to -- to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not correct. The Serb artillery had precise plans that had been drawn up much earlier. I don't know wanted to elaborate now. But they had precisely prepared plans on what it was that it had to be destroyed in case an attack was to occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you just show us the parts of town that were shelled on the day of the attack.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, Stari Grad, Zagrad and the Partizanska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just mark in red -- I think have you a red marker there. All right. If you don't, just mark those parts that you were just mentioning.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, here, this part and then this part, along the Sava [as interpreted] river, and in the very centre of town, we called it Carsija, old town, where there were old shops, hundreds of years old, with old -- old craft shops of Muslims and Croats held by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please enter this into evidence and get a number assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D96. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic again before we proceed, I must admit I still fail to see how all of this, as interesting as it is, is relevant to the charges raised against your client in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief charges my client as part of the JCE, a large-scale attack on Prijedor, among others Stari Grad and these other parts where the fighting on the 30th of May occurred, and the Defence is trying to put in context this attack and the response by the Serb forces or Serb army. But I will move on to that somewhat later. I will ask about who ordered the attacks and how it proceeded and so on, because it is the Prosecutor's claim that this attack was completely unprovoked, that it was a widespread attack on civilian, on a civilian population and this is why I am putting these questions to the witness because he testified about this aspect in the Stakic case but he did not fully explain the entire situation, as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I could see this coming from you as an explanation as to why you think it would be relevant. But I need not remind you that tu quoque is not a legitimate Defence in these trials, and therefore I don't think that -- that it makes much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That is not my intention at all. I'm merely drawing a context or -- for an attack and a counter-attack. It was a military operation carried out by local brigade commander by the name of Zeljaja, who had nothing to do with Mr. Zupljanin. That was my line of questions. We reached a moment of attack and we were about to discuss the participants in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, this was all to draw certain context. And you mentioned that the plan was arranged between Zeljaja and Hadzija.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: And Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the artillery army units which shelled the old town and which carried out the attack?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that they had been deployed much before these events in Prijedor, after the Serb army withdrew from the Croatian theatre. Most of the arsenal of weapons was deployed around Prijedor. Prijedor was a majority Muslim town located at a very important transit route between the Serbian Krajina and the Krajina in Croatia. It was along that route and that town had to be taken over at any cost by the Serbs. That's what Karadzic said on the 12th of May at the well-known Assembly meeting in Banja Luka. He ordered this to be done to the Prijedor police and army leadership, that Prijedor needs to be taken as -- as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What area of responsibility was this? Of what brigade?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That morning, when the fighting broke out there Prijedor, there were basically all brigades there, which had to do with the Prijedor Barracks. There were members of the 5th Kozarac Brigade and the 34th Motorised Brigade, some members of the Sana Brigade arrived to assist as well as people from Bosanski Novi. There was this notorious group called Spare Ribs. They committed atrocious crimes on the left bank of the Sava. And they all co-operated with the Prijedor police led by Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic, Milutin Cadzo and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the 5th Kozara Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Pero Colic. It was well-known for their crimes in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about the 35th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, it used to be the 343rd and then it was the 34th Brigade. I think Arsic and Zeljaja were commanders. They rotated. I know that Radmilo Zeljaja was basically the person in charge. He was an intelligence officer with an intensive military intelligence background. He was the main person in all of these events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further in your testimony when you spoke about another attack in the Stakic case, you mentioned Hambarine. You commented on a news article from Kozarski Vjesnik. Do you remember that? You were shown this by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it preceded the ethnic cleansing in Prijedor. The Hambarine events took place on 22nd of May in Hambarinsko Polje. A civilian vehicle was stopped carrying six well-armed Serb soldiers. There was still a decree in force at the time issued by the legal authorities at the municipal level in Prijedor, stating that in the enclave where the Muslims were in the majority, there had to be check-points formed which were to serve to check any Serb soldiers who frequently tried to enter the enclave drunk and to prevent them from doing so. They were supposed to hand over their weapons at such check-points and on their way out they would be given their weapons back. Although the Serbs had taken over Prijedor by that time that vehicle was still stopped in Hambarinsko Polje. The six drunk Serb soldiers in a single car caused an incident. The patrolmen at the check-point asked them to surrender their weapons, promising that they would return them once they came back. However, the people in the vehicle opened fire and the result was two dead Serb soldiers and a number of wounded. As for those manning the check-point, they also sustained some casualties. There was number of wounded. The next day the Serb authorities seized that opportunity to announce over Radio Prijedor or to issue an ultimatum to the Hambarine residents to hand over Mr. Saliskovic, who had been an active-duty policeman, who, on that day, manned the check-point alongside some others. Since that did not occur, on the 23rd, at 2.30 p.m., they used long-range artillery from the Prijedor airport at Topica Brdo, which is a feature, this artillery had come from the Croatian theatre, and they used it to shell and destroy Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, is it not correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we have reached the point where we would take the -- we would rise for the day. How much longer do you expect that you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention in the transcript, 86, 17, I believe it is recorded he said an ultimatum and that is not the word that the witness used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Should the -- should counsel ask the question again to get the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to preserve the record so he can ask tomorrow or we can ask for some verification requests. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment until tomorrow. I believe from the last thing I read that we're in this courtroom every day this week. So we would resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. I must tell the witness that notwithstanding what I said earlier about being completed today, unfortunately you have to return tomorrow. And therefore, I am to remind you that having been sworn as a witness, you can't have any communication with counsel from either side, nor can you discuss your testimony with anybody outside the court. So we continue at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of August, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.
